title: How Indigenous Psychologies Resemble Mathematics: The Epistemic Role of Conceptual Innovation.
abstract: This paper argues that indigenous psychologies and mathematics share an important methodological feature: both advance understanding by refining conceptual systems and terminology. Throughout the history of mathematics, the reformulation of concepts has often enabled mathematicians to solve problems that had remained unresolved for centuries. Similarly, indigenous psychologies emerged from the recognition that the concepts of mainstream psychology do not always adequately capture the psychological realities of indigenous populations. They therefore develop culturally grounded concepts and terminology that improve the understanding of psychological phenomena within specific cultural contexts. Most indigenous psychology concepts belong to the field of social psychology. If the primary goal of social psychology is to understand human social behavior and experience, then indigenous psychologies pursue this goal through conceptual innovation in much the same way that mathematics advances through the refinement of its own conceptual framework. The paper also identifies important limits to this analogy: unlike mathematical concepts, the usefulness of indigenous psychological concepts may be difficult to appreciate without experience of the relevant cultural environment. The paper therefore discusses cultural experience and social success as possible ways of assessing the value of indigenous psychological concepts.
